Under [A1], apply [F1] to the KLR datum in the Given. Its hypotheses are
the datum and field specified in [F2], and its conclusion is exactly the
isomorphism $\gamma_D:A f_D\to K_0(R_D)$ with the Laurent grading parameter
$q_{\mathrm{gr}}$. This use makes no claim about a representation on the
spin spaces.

In $V(1)$, $H$ has eigenvalue $1$ on $|\uparrow\rangle$ and $-1$ on
$|\downarrow\rangle$. The elementary tensor basis of $V(1)^{\otimes n}$
therefore consists of $H$-eigenvectors. A tensor with exactly $k$ down
factors has eigenvalue $n-2k$, and there are exactly $\binom nk$ such
tensors. Hence its weight character is
$(z+z^{-1})^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk z^{n-2k}$.

The monomials $x^{n-k}y^k$ form a basis of $V(n)$. Applying
$H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y$ gives
$H(x^{n-k}y^k)=(n-2k)x^{n-k}y^k$, so each listed weight space is
one-dimensional. For $k>0$, $E(x^{n-k}y^k)=k x^{n-k+1}y^{k-1}$ is nonzero;
for $k<n$, $F(x^{n-k}y^k)=(n-k)x^{n-k-1}y^{k+1}$ is nonzero. Any nonzero
submodule has a nonzero $H$-weight vector, since the eigenvalues are distinct
and the corresponding projections are polynomials in $H$. Repeated $E$
then reaches $x^n$, and repeated $F$ from $x^n$ reaches every basis
monomial. Thus $V(n)$ is irreducible and its weights have multiplicity one.

On a tensor basis vector with $k$ down factors,
$S_n^z$ has eigenvalue $(n-2k)/2$, so $H_n^{(0)}$ has eigenvalue
$-h(n-2k)/2$. Summing the exponentials over the basis gives
$$ Z_n(\beta)=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk e^{\beta h(n-2k)/2} =\bigl(e^{\beta h/2}+e^{-\beta h/2}\bigr)^n =\bigl(2\cosh(\beta h/2)\bigr)^n. $$
This is an exact finite-matrix trace identity for the stated operator.

The isomorphism in [F1] identifies $A f_D$ with $K_0(R_D)$ only.
For $n\geq2$, the weight $n-2$ has multiplicity $n$ in step 1.2 and
multiplicity one in step 1.3, so the two characters differ; for $n=1$ they
coincide. The map in [F1] assigns neither module to its Grothendieck group.
Likewise, [F1] has no Hamiltonian operator, while step 2.1 computes the trace
only after $H_n^{(0)}$ is specified. A tensor-product categorical action or
a spin-chain spectrum therefore requires additional data.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

an endomorphism of $V$, let $A_j$ act as $A$ on factor $j$ and as the identity
on the other factors. Define the diagonal generators
$$ S_N^+=\sum_{j=1}^N E_j,\qquad S_N^-=\sum_{j=1}^N F_j,\qquad S_N^z=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N H_j. $$

algebraic spin convention.

$P(A\otimes I)P=I\otimes A$ and $P(I\otimes A)P=A\otimes I$. Hence
$P(A\otimes I+I\otimes A)=(A\otimes I+I\otimes A)P$. The same identity on
factors $i,j$, while $P_{ij}$ commutes with every $A_k$ for $k\ne i,j$,
proves the three displayed commutators for $A=E,F,H/2$. This is a direct
matrix identity under the inherited assumption [A1] and the spin definition
[F1].

For $N\geq3$, every term in $H_N$ from [F3] is a real scalar multiple
of a swap $P_{ij}$, including the periodic bond $P_{N,1}$, and the identity
term commutes with every endomorphism. Step 1.1 therefore gives
$[H_N,S_N^+]=[H_N,S_N^-]=[H_N,S_N^z]=0$. Each swap is a unitary involution
on the standard tensor-product inner product, hence $P_{ij}^*=P_{ij}$;
the real linear combination $H_N$ is Hermitian.

On $V_a\otimes\mathcal H_N$, the flip $P_{aj}$ commutes with
$A_a+\sum_{k=1}^N A_k$ for each $A\in\{E,F,H/2\}$: the two-factor flip
identity from step 1.1 applies to $A_a+A_j$, and $P_{aj}$ commutes with
$A_k$ for $k\ne j$. Thus $R_{aj}(u)=uI+iP_{aj}$ commutes with this total
generator. A product of operators commuting with a fixed operator also
commutes with it, since $[XY,G]=X[Y,G]+[X,G]Y$. Hence $T_a(u)$ commutes
with $A_a+\sum_kA_k$.

The finite partial trace is cyclic for an endomorphism acting only on
$V_a$. In an auxiliary basis, write $X=(X_{rs})$ in chain-operator blocks
and $A=(A_{rs})$ in scalar entries. Then
$\operatorname{tr}_a((A_a\otimes I)X)=\sum_{r,s}A_{rs}X_{sr}$ and
$\operatorname{tr}_a(X(A_a\otimes I))=\sum_{r,s}X_{rs}A_{sr}$; relabelling
$r,s$ in the second sum and commuting scalar coefficients shows equality.
Taking $\operatorname{tr}_a$ of
$[A_a+\sum_kA_k,T_a(u)]=0$ therefore gives
$[\sum_kA_k,\operatorname{tr}_aT_a(u)]=0$: the chain generators act only on
the untraced tensor factors, so their commutator passes through
$\operatorname{tr}_a$. With $t(u)$ as in [F2], this is each asserted
transfer-matrix commutator.

By [F1], $S_N^z$ is diagonal in the tensor basis with eigenvalues
$-N/2,-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2$, so its weight spaces form an orthogonal direct
sum of $\mathcal H_N$. Since $[H_N,S_N^z]=0$ by step 2.1, each
$\mathcal H_{N,m}$ is invariant under $H_N$ and under every power $H_N^r$.
For a finite-dimensional operator norm,
$\sum_{r\geq0}\|(-\beta H_N)^r/r!\|
\leq e^{|\beta|\|H_N\|}<\infty$, so the exponential series converges in
operator norm. Its partial sums preserve every $\mathcal H_{N,m}$, and their
limits do as well because these subspaces are closed. The exponential is
therefore block diagonal for the orthogonal decomposition
$\mathcal H_N=\bigoplus_m\mathcal H_{N,m}$. In a basis formed by concatenating
orthonormal bases of the blocks, the matrix trace is the sum of the block
traces, giving the stated identity.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$V=\mathbb C^2$ with ordered orthonormal basis $|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle$.

$$ E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$
They satisfy $[H,E]=2E$, $[H,F]=-2F$, and $[E,F]=H$, and therefore define
the standard two-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$.
Write $S^+=E$, $S^-=F$, and $S^z=H/2$.

$\mathcal H_N=V^{\otimes N}$ with its tensor-product inner product. If $A$ is
an endomorphism of $V$, let $A_j$ act as $A$ on factor $j$ and as the identity
on the other factors. Define the diagonal generators
$$ S_N^+=\sum_{j=1}^N E_j,\qquad S_N^-=\sum_{j=1}^N F_j,\qquad S_N^z=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N H_j. $$
For $m\in\{-N/2,-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2\}$, its weight space is
$\mathcal H_{N,m}=\ker(S_N^z-mI)$. These are dimensionless matrices in the
algebraic spin convention.

For each integer $r\geq0$, define $V(r)$ to be the vector space
$\mathbb C[x,y]_r$ of homogeneous polynomials of degree $r$, with
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ action
$$ E=x\partial_y,\qquad F=y\partial_x,\qquad H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y. $$
The ordered monomials $x^{r-k}y^k$ for $0\leq k\leq r$ form its basis.
Under $x\mapsto|\uparrow\rangle$ and $y\mapsto|\downarrow\rangle$,
$V(1)$ is the representation on $V$ above. A tensor power $V(1)^{\otimes N}$
uses the diagonal action defined by the sums $S_N^+,S_N^-,2S_N^z$.

cardinality. Put $\nu=\sqrt{q_H}>1$ and $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)$. The representation category of
the one-vertex, no-arrow quiver over $\mathbb F_{q_H}$ is the category of
finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_{q_H}$-vector spaces, with unique simple object
$S=\mathbb F_{q_H}$. Its Hall composition algebra is the subalgebra generated
by the class $[S]$ in the twisted Hall algebra with the normalization of the
Ringel supplier. The rank-one positive quantum half is
$U_\nu^+(\mathfrak{sl}_2)=K[E]$. The canonical Ringel map $E\mapsto[S]$
identifies this positive half with the composition algebra; the finite-Dynkin
criterion identifies it with the full Hall algebra in this one-vertex case.
